about: R19 narration scripts for the seeded fictional companies' deck videos. Written by hand from each company's seeded deck (apps/q-api/src/dev/fictional-world/companies.ts); no figure beyond the seed. One segment per deck slide, in slide order. Narrated by the q-api one-way speech route; every video is labelled AI-narrated.

segments.text: This is Ledgerfold, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Ledgerfold lends working capital to Lagos market traders, underwritten from the bookkeeping app they use every day.
The app is free. After ninety days of records it offers fourteen to sixty day loans, repaid from daily sales through agency-banking partners.
The founders size the market at around three million traders in Lagos State.
Revenue is interest and a flat facility fee on each loan.
They report sixty-four hundred traders keeping books in the app, and twenty-one hundred and fifty who have borrowed.
The loan book is reported to have grown from one hundred and fifty thousand dollars in September 2025 to four hundred and ten thousand in March 2026.
Monthly revenue is about thirty-eight thousand dollars, with thirty-day portfolio at risk of three point eight percent.
The CEO ran SME lending operations for five years; the CTO built payments back-ends.
Next: a debt partner for on-lending, a risk team, and the Onitsha and Aba markets.
Ledgerfold is raising two and a half million dollars in a priced seed. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Tarmacly, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Tarmacly is a middle-mile freight marketplace on the Kano, Lagos and Port Harcourt corridors.
Shippers post loads. Tarmacly matches vetted trucks, prices and tracks the trip, and confirms delivery. Carriers are paid within forty-eight hours through a partner bank.
The company describes Nigerian road freight as a twenty billion dollar a year market, mostly still booked by phone.
It earns a take rate of around nine percent per trip, plus a financing margin on early carrier payment.
It reports one hundred and eighty shippers under contract and twenty-three hundred onboarded trucks.
Completed trips are reported rising from eight hundred and twenty in September 2025 to fourteen hundred and fifty in March 2026.
Three founders cover fleet operations, FMCG distribution and engineering, with sixty-four staff in three cities.
Next: the Abuja to Onitsha corridor and route-level pricing.
Tarmacly is raising an eight million dollar Series A. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Yamfield Agro, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Yamfield puts solar cold rooms at rural Benue markets, and buys stored produce at a floor price.
Farmers rent container cold rooms per crate per day, and pay by mobile money.
The problem it names: farmers lose thirty to forty percent of their tomatoes after harvest, for lack of nearby cold storage.
Revenue comes from storage fees per crate, plus a trading margin on produce bought at the floor price.
Two pilot cold rooms have run since August 2025, and three hundred and ten farmers have stored produce. It is early, and unit economics per site are not yet proven.
The CEO ran post-harvest loss programmes for four years. The engineering co-founder is part-time.
The plan is eight more cold rooms in Benue, then Nasarawa, once each site's economics are proven.
Yamfield is raising four hundred thousand dollars on a SAFE to build eight cold rooms. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Clinicrest, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Clinicrest keeps primary clinics stocked with genuine essential medicines, delivered next day.
A tablet inventory app forecasts each clinic's needs, and is tied to a licensed warehouse in Ibadan.
The company counts around thirty thousand private medicine outlets in south-west Nigeria.
It earns a distribution margin on medicines, plus a monthly software subscription per clinic.
It reports two hundred and twelve paying clinic and pharmacy accounts in February 2026.
Monthly revenue was about ninety-five thousand dollars that month.
A physician CEO and a pharmaceutical-distribution COO lead the team, with two licensed pharmacists on staff.
Next: depots in Abeokuta and Osogbo, and credit terms for clinics.
Clinicrest is raising one point eight million dollars in a priced seed. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Marketlight Grids, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Marketlight replaces diesel generators in Nigerian markets with solar mini-grids.
Every shop gets a prepaid smart meter, topped up by mobile money, on solar and battery mini-grids.
The company says traders pay roughly three times grid prices for generator power.
It charges per kilowatt-hour under fifteen-year concessions with market associations, and owns the assets.
Live mini-grids are reported growing from six in March 2024 to fourteen in March 2026.
Annualised revenue is about one point nine million dollars, with a collection rate of ninety-six percent.
An engineer CEO from rural electrification and a project-finance CFO lead fifty-eight staff.
The plan is thirty more mini-grids across the North Central zone, financed with equity and project debt.
Marketlight is raising twelve million dollars in equity, alongside a separate debt facility. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Tallyloom, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Tallyloom runs payroll and statutory compliance for mid-sized employers in Nigeria and Ghana.
It computes and files PAYE, pension and NHF, pays staff through bank integrations, and keeps an inspection-ready audit trail.
The company counts around sixty thousand formal employers with twenty to a thousand staff across the two countries.
Pricing is per employee per month, with HR modules as an upsell.
It reports twelve hundred and fifty employers paying for one hundred and eighty-six thousand seats, and net revenue retention of one hundred and eighteen percent.
Annual recurring revenue is reported at two point one million dollars in 2023, rising to six point four million in December 2025.
A second-time founder CEO with nine years in payroll outsourcing leads one hundred and forty staff in Lagos and Accra.
Next: Kenya, embedded salary advances with a bank partner, and enterprise sales.
Tallyloom is raising a twenty-two million dollar Series B. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Ajopot, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Ajopot digitises ajo, the rotating savings circle, with members' funds held at a licensed partner bank.
Each circle has a fixed payout order and auto-debited contributions, and every member carries a reliability score.
Today it charges a one percent fee on each payout. Small loans against circle history come next.
It reports fifty-two thousand registered users in thirty-nine hundred circles.
Monthly active users are reported rising from forty-two hundred in September 2025 to eighteen thousand seven hundred in March 2026.
A product-growth CEO from a driver-wallet app and an engineering CTO lead fourteen staff.
Next: Abuja and Port Harcourt, and small loans against circle history.
Ajopot is raising one point two billion naira on a SAFE for growth and lending. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Maji Loop, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Maji Loop sells clean water by the litre from solar-pumped, metered kiosks in Nairobi.
Each kiosk combines solar pumping, filtration and a smart dispenser. Residents pay by M-Pesa or with a tag.
The company notes that more than two million people live in Nairobi's informal settlements.
It sells per litre, sharing revenue with the utility under a service contract.
Live kiosks are reported growing from thirty-eight in 2023 to ninety-six in 2025.
A water-engineer CEO from a county utility and an embedded-hardware CTO lead twenty-two staff.
The plan is one hundred and fifty more kiosks in Nairobi and Mombasa.
Maji Loop is raising one and a half million dollars in a priced seed to build them. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Nsuo Labs, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Nsuo Labs makes ice with solar power at Ghana's landing beaches, and rents insulated crates to fish traders, to cut spoilage between the canoe and the market.
A beach-side solar ice plant supplies crates, rented per day through trader groups.
It reports one hundred and forty regular trader customers at its pilot site in Tema.
Traders there report spoilage falling from about twenty-five percent of the catch to under ten. That is the traders' own account, from a single site.
The founder is a refrigeration engineer with four staff. A co-founder hire is planned, so the team is not yet complete.
Next: five more beach sites along the Greater Accra and Central coasts.
Nsuo Labs is raising six hundred thousand dollars on a SAFE, for five sites and a co-founder. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Brightkloof Energy, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Brightkloof puts solar and batteries on South African SME rooftops for a fixed monthly fee, with no upfront cost, designed around load-shedding.
Design, installation, monitoring and maintenance are included for ten years.
The company says several hundred thousand SMEs have rooftops suitable for solar.
It sells ten-year subscriptions, later sold into securitised pools to recycle capital.
It reports twenty-nine hundred SME sites and thirty-eight megawatts peak installed.
Contracted annual recurring revenue is reported at ninety-six million rand in FY2023, rising to two hundred and fourteen million in FY2025.
A former energy banker CEO and an electrical-engineering CTO lead two hundred and ten staff, with in-house crews.
Next: KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, and securitising mature contracts.
Brightkloof is raising two hundred and eighty million rand in Series B equity. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Souqsheet, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Souqsheet gives Cairo's neighbourhood kiosks one app to order from every distributor, track stock and get supplier credit.
It runs on Android: ordering across distributors, simple stock tracking, and seven-day supplier credit through a partner bank.
Revenue is distributor subscription fees, plus a margin on supplier credit.
It reports ninety-eight hundred kiosks ordering every month across Greater Cairo and Alexandria.
Gross order value is reported rising from one point six million dollars a month in February 2024 to four point two million in February 2026.
An FMCG trade-marketing CEO and an engineering CTO lead seventy-five staff.
Next: Upper Egypt, and scaling supplier credit.
Souqsheet is raising a six million dollar Series A. These figures are the company's own claims.
This is Kazikit, a fictional demo company, summarised by Q from its own deck.
Kazikit helps Kenya's informal building contractors, the fundis, quote, cost and get paid from a basic Android phone.
Contractors build quotes with local material prices, track spend on each job, and send M-Pesa payment requests.
There is no revenue yet. A paid tier is planned from mid-2026, with a materials marketplace alongside hardware stores.
It reports nineteen hundred contractors signed up since September 2025, and about six hundred using it weekly.
A software-engineer CTO and a CEO who ran a hardware chain's credit desk lead the company.
Kazikit is raising three hundred and fifty thousand dollars on a SAFE, for the paid tier and the marketplace. These figures are the company's own claims.
